body: ## Best Korean Skincare for PIH: How to Fade Post-Acne Dark Spots ### Quick Answer **Question:** Which Korean skincare products and ingredients actually fade PIH (post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation), the brown or tan marks left behind after acne? **Answer:** PIH is excess melanin left in the skin after inflammation, so it responds to ingredients that interrupt pigment production rather than the barrier-calming ingredients used for red marks. The most effective options in Korean skincare are [tranexamic acid](https://www.seoulsister.com/ingredients/tranexamic-acid), [niacinamide](https://www.seoulsister.com/ingredients/niacinamide), [alpha-arbutin](https://www.seoulsister.com/ingredients/arbutin), and [vitamin C](https://www.seoulsister.com/ingredients/ascorbic-acid), paired with daily sunscreen that is genuinely non-negotiable. Without sun protection, every one of those actives is working against a force that re-darkens the spot faster than it can fade. Most people see meaningful change between 8 and 16 weeks. **Jump to what you need:** - [Best Korean Serum for PIH](#best-serum-for-pih) - [Best Korean Toner for PIH](#best-toner-for-pih) - [Best Korean Essence or Ampoule for PIH](#best-essence-for-pih) - [The Ingredients That Actually Move PIH](#best-ingredients-for-pih) - [A Realistic Timeline](#how-long) - [Frequently Asked Questions](#faq) ## First, Make Sure You Actually Have PIH This is the step almost everyone skips, and getting it wrong costs months. Look at the marks in natural light, not bathroom lighting. Are they **brown, tan, or grayish**? Or are they **pink, red, or purple**? If they are brown, you have PIH, and this guide is for you. If they are red or pink, you have PIE (post-inflammatory erythema), which is a completely different problem. PIE is damaged blood vessels, not pigment, and the brightening ingredients in this article will do very little for it. Read our dedicated guide on [Korean skincare for PIE acne scars and texture](https://www.seoulsister.com/blog/best-korean-skincare-for-pie-acne-scars-and-texture) instead. There is a quick physical test that settles it. Press a clear drinking glass gently against the mark. If the color **temporarily disappears** under the pressure and floods back when you release, that is PIE, because you are squeezing blood out of dilated vessels. If the mark **stays exactly the same color** under pressure, that is PIH, because melanin does not move when you press on it. It is entirely possible to have both at once, often from the same breakout. If you do, treat them as two separate projects rather than hunting for one product that claims to fix everything. ## Why PIH Happens, and Why Some People Get It More When a pimple becomes inflamed, the inflammation signals your melanocytes, the pigment-producing cells in your skin, to ramp up melanin output in that spot. Once the acne clears, that extra melanin stays behind in the tissue. It is not a scar in the structural sense. There is no lost collagen, no indentation. It is a pigment deposit sitting in skin that is otherwise fully healed, which is genuinely good news, because pigment can be broken down and cleared. Real scars cannot. Two things make PIH worse and more stubborn. **The first is picking.** Every time you squeeze or pick at a spot, you extend and intensify the inflammation, and the pigment response scales with it. A pimple you leave alone might leave a faint mark for six weeks. The same pimple picked at for three days can leave a mark that lasts a year. **The second is sun exposure.** UV light directly stimulates the same melanocytes that are already overproducing. This is why PIH often looks worse in late summer than it did in spring, and it is why sunscreen is not a nice-to-have in a PIH routine but the foundation the entire routine sits on. There is also a factor worth naming directly, because most Western skincare advice glosses over it: **deeper skin tones are more prone to PIH, and it tends to be darker and longer-lasting.** More active melanocytes means a stronger pigment response to the same amount of inflammation. If this is your skin, the practical implications are that early intervention matters more, aggressive treatments carry more risk (harsh exfoliation and irritation can trigger *more* pigment, making things worse), and gentle-but-consistent beats fast-and-strong every time. Korean skincare happens to be well suited to this, because the formulation philosophy leans toward sustained gentle actives rather than high-percentage single hits. ## Best Korean Serum for PIH The serum step is where the pigment work actually happens, because it is the most concentrated leave-on layer in the routine. For PIH you want tranexamic acid, niacinamide, or arbutin sitting near the top of the ingredient list rather than decorating the bottom of it, where a "brightening serum" often puts them. **Top pick: [Numbuzin No.5+ Vitamin Concentrated Serum](https://www.seoulsister.com/products/2d041fc2-78b2-4d03-98f1-d0511b3b76bd)** (4.7 stars across roughly 5,400 reviews, see the current price). Its verified ingredient list carries niacinamide and panthenol at 50,000ppm each and tranexamic acid at 40,000ppm, all in the top five ingredients, with alpha-arbutin further down. That is two separate pigment pathways addressed in one step, plus a soothing agent to offset the irritation risk that would otherwise feed the problem. For most people with PIH this is the single most efficient bottle on this page. **Higher-strength alternate: [Anua Niacinamide 10% + TXA 4% Dark Spot Correcting Serum](https://www.seoulsister.com/products/da04f946-d191-4dda-8662-1e36a860bc17)** (4.7 stars across roughly 960 reviews, see the current price). The percentages are on the label and they hold up on the ingredient list: niacinamide at 10% and tranexamic acid at 4%, positions three and four, with both arbutin and alpha-arbutin present as well. Worth naming the tradeoff honestly, though. Niacinamide at 10% causes flushing in a meaningful minority of people, and on PIH irritation is not a neutral side effect. If you have never used niacinamide before, start with the Numbuzin and move here only if you plateau. **Sensitive-skin alternate: [Dr. Althea Vitamin C Boosting Serum](https://www.seoulsister.com/products/79eb221d-1525-401d-98eb-7f39182e0967)** (4.7 stars across roughly 550 reviews, see the current price). This one leads with centella asiatica leaf water and niacinamide, carries tranexamic acid at position eleven, and gets its vitamin C from 3-O-ethyl ascorbic acid, a derivative that is far less reactive than pure L-ascorbic acid. If straight vitamin C serums have stung or flushed your skin before, this is the gentler way into the same category. **The honest limitation:** a serum does not remove pigment that is already sitting in your skin. It slows or interrupts the production of new melanin and lets your natural cell turnover clear what is already there, which takes months rather than weeks. Nothing in this section works at all without daily sunscreen, because UV re-darkens the spot faster than any of these actives can fade it. ## Best Korean Toner for PIH The toner step is the one people most often waste on PIH. A hydrating toner that contains nothing for pigment is a fine product and does nothing for your dark spots. If you are going to use this step, make it carry an active, because it is applied to damp skin across the whole face and that is a genuinely useful delivery position for a brightener. **Top pick: [Numbuzin No. 5+ Vitamin Boosting Essential Toner](https://www.seoulsister.com/products/9a90d4b4-60d9-4991-814e-30c5f342ccbc)** (4.7 stars across roughly 630 reviews, see the current price). Niacinamide sits at position four and 3-O-ethyl ascorbic acid at thirteen, with madecassoside and panthenol further down to keep it comfortable. Note the naming carefully: this is the No. 5+ *toner*, a different product from the No.5+ *serum* above. In a numbered Korean line the number is the whole identity, and these two get confused constantly. **Gentler alternate: [Anua Rice 70 Glow Milky Toner](https://www.seoulsister.com/products/ce2183fe-0cc3-4b61-a280-401b45c384a4)** (4.8 stars across roughly 370 reviews, see the current price). Niacinamide at position five in a milky rice base that is closer to a light essence than a traditional toner. Being straight with you about the label: it does list arbutin and ascorbic acid, but both sit in the low thirties out of thirty-eight ingredients, which is trace territory. Buy this for the niacinamide and the comfort, not for the arbutin. **The honest limitation:** no toner is going to be the product that fades your PIH. This step is a support layer at genuinely low concentrations, and if your budget only stretches to one active product, it should be the serum, not this. A toner earns its place by making the routine pleasant enough that you actually keep doing it for the three months this takes. ## Best Korean Essence or Ampoule for PIH Essences and ampoules sit between toner and serum, and for PIH the useful ones are the ampoules that behave like a second concentrated treatment step rather than a hydrating layer. This is the step to add when a serum alone has stalled, not the step to start with. **Top pick: [SKIN1004 Madagascar Centella Tone Brightening Capsule Ampoule](https://www.seoulsister.com/products/baffcc1e-eff8-4228-b169-130c0e329b64)** (4.7 stars across roughly 820 reviews, see the current price). Niacinamide at position three and tranexamic acid at five, with centella asiatica extract, madecassoside, and panthenol carrying the soothing side. That combination is well matched to PIH specifically, because it pairs the two pigment actives that are best tolerated by reactive skin with the calming ingredients that keep irritation from generating more pigment while you treat it. **Sensitive-skin alternate: [SKIN1004 Madagascar Centella Soothing Cream](https://www.seoulsister.com/products/1bf18471-7fdf-4748-bf54-6161577680f1)** (4.8 stars across roughly 1,250 reviews, see the current price). Be clear about what this is and is not. It is centella at 72% as the first ingredient with tranexamic acid much further down, so it is a barrier and calming product, not a brightener. It goes here because if your skin is currently flaring, the correct first move on PIH is to calm it and repair the barrier before adding any pigment active at all. Irritated skin makes more pigment. Starting aggressively on reactive skin is counterproductive rather than merely uncomfortable. **The honest limitation:** an essence or ampoule is an addition, not a replacement. If you are already using a tranexamic acid or niacinamide serum, adding one of these gives you a modest increase in exposure to the same actives, not a new mechanism. Stacking four brightening products at once is a reliable way to compromise your barrier and end up with more pigment than you started with, so add this step only once the serum is comfortable and you have given it several weeks. ## The Ingredients That Actually Move PIH **1. Tranexamic acid, the most underrated of the group** [Tranexamic acid](https://www.seoulsister.com/ingredients/tranexamic-acid) works differently from most brighteners. Rather than only inhibiting the pigment-making enzyme, it interrupts the signaling between your skin cells and melanocytes, essentially quieting the message that tells them to produce more pigment. That makes it particularly useful for inflammation-driven pigment like PIH. It is also well tolerated by skin that reacts badly to vitamin C. *Grounded pick:* **Numbuzin No.5+ Vitamin Concentrated Serum** (4.7 stars across roughly 5,400 reviews, see the current price). Its verified ingredient list carries tranexamic acid at 40,000ppm (4%) alongside niacinamide at 50,000ppm (5%) and panthenol at the same level, which is a genuinely efficient combination for PIH: you get two different pigment pathways addressed in one step, plus a soothing agent to offset the irritation risk that would otherwise feed the problem. **2. Niacinamide, the one that blocks pigment transfer** [Niacinamide](https://www.seoulsister.com/ingredients/niacinamide) does not stop melanin being made. It stops it being *delivered*, blocking the transfer of pigment from melanocytes into the surface skin cells where you actually see it. It also strengthens the barrier, which matters more than it sounds: a compromised barrier is more easily irritated, and irritation is what generates PIH in the first place. *Grounded picks:* **Numbuzin No.3 Skin Softening Serum** (check the current price and stock; the No.5 pad next to it is an alternative), which pairs niacinamide with fermented ingredients that support turnover gently, or the **Numbuzin No.5 Vitamin-Niacinamide Concentrated Pad** (4.6 stars across roughly 6,800 reviews, see the current price) if you prefer a pad format. Both sit at moderate strength, which is deliberate: high-percentage niacinamide causes flushing and irritation in a meaningful minority of people, and with PIH, irritation is not a neutral side effect. It actively feeds the problem you are treating. If you see a 20% niacinamide serum on a shelf and assume it must be twice as good as a 5%, that is the assumption to drop. There is no prize for starting high. **3. Alpha-arbutin and vitamin C, the classic brighteners** [Alpha-arbutin](https://www.seoulsister.com/ingredients/arbutin) is a gentler relative of hydroquinone that inhibits tyrosinase, the enzyme that produces melanin. [Vitamin C](https://www.seoulsister.com/ingredients/ascorbic-acid) does the same while adding antioxidant protection that helps limit new UV-triggered pigment during the day. Vitamin C is the more irritating of the two, so it is the one to introduce slowly. *Grounded pick:* **Beauty of Joseon Glow Deep Serum: Rice + Alpha-Arbutin** (4.6 stars across roughly 5,800 reviews, see the current price). Alpha-arbutin is right there in the name and on the label rather than buried, and the rice base keeps it mild enough for daily use. For a vitamin C that will not sting, the **Neogen Dermalogy Real Vita C Serum** (4.5 stars across roughly 4,200 reviews, see the current price) leads with sodium ascorbyl phosphate, a derivative that sits near neutral pH instead of the low pH that makes pure L-ascorbic acid so reactive. **4. Targeted treatments for individual stubborn spots** Some marks lag behind the rest. Spot treatments concentrate actives on a small area rather than across the whole face. We are deliberately not naming a single spot-treatment pick here. The dedicated dark-spot pads and patches in our catalog do not yet have enough verified review volume behind them for us to call one a confident recommendation, and on a category where the alternative is simply using your existing serum more precisely, we would rather say that than fill the gap with a name. What works without buying anything new: apply your brightening serum to the whole area, then go back over the individual marks with a second small pass. Concentration on the spot is most of what a dedicated spot product is selling you. If a mark is still raised, red, or tender, it has not become PIH yet, so treat the blemish first rather than layering brighteners onto active inflammation. **5. A gentler entry point if all of the above is too much** If your skin reacts to almost everything, start with a soothing base rather than a brightening active, and add the pigment work only once your barrier is comfortable. Irritated skin makes more pigment, so an aggressive start on reactive skin is genuinely counterproductive rather than merely uncomfortable. *Grounded pick:* **Beplain Cicaful Calming Ampoule** (4.7 stars across roughly 6,800 reviews, see the current price) for a centella-led calming step, or the **Illiyoon Ceramide Ato Concentrate Cream** (roughly 15,200 reviews, see the current price) if what you need is barrier repair before anything else. Neither will fade a spot on its own. That is the point: they make it possible to tolerate the thing that will. **6. Sunscreen, which is not optional here** Every ingredient above is trying to reduce pigment. UV exposure is trying to increase it, and UV is stronger and faster. Skipping sunscreen while using brighteners is close to pointless. Wear it daily, including indoors near windows and on overcast days, and reapply if you are outside for extended periods. If you take one thing from this article and ignore the rest, take this one. ## A Realistic Timeline PIH fades on a schedule measured in months, and knowing that up front prevents the routine-hopping that resets your progress every six weeks. **Weeks 1 to 4:** Very little visible change in the marks themselves. Your skin should feel more even in texture and hydration. This is the phase where most people quit. **Weeks 4 to 8:** The newest and lightest marks begin to fade. Older, darker spots stay put. If you photograph your skin in consistent lighting, the change is measurable here even when the mirror suggests otherwise. **Weeks 8 to 16:** The meaningful improvement window. Moderate marks lighten substantially, and the overall tone starts to even out. **Beyond 16 weeks:** Deep or long-standing PIH, particularly on deeper skin tones, can take six months to a year. This is normal and is not evidence your routine is failing. Two things dramatically extend every number above: inconsistent sunscreen, and continuing to pick at active breakouts. Both are within your control, and both matter more than which serum you chose. ## What to Avoid **Aggressive exfoliation.** Scrubs, high-percentage peels, and daily acids feel productive but cause irritation, and irritation causes PIH. This risk is higher on deeper skin tones. Gentle chemical exfoliation once or twice a week is plenty. **Stacking every brightener at once.** Using tranexamic acid, arbutin, vitamin C, and a strong exfoliant simultaneously does not produce faster results. It produces a compromised barrier and, often, more pigment. Pick two, use them consistently, add a third only if your skin is comfortable after several weeks. **Treating an active breakout as PIH.** If the spot is still raised, red, or tender, it is not PIH yet. Calm the acne first. Brighteners on inflamed skin add irritation to inflammation. **Judging progress in bathroom mirrors.** Overhead bathroom lighting exaggerates shadows and unevenness. Use the same natural-light spot at the same time of day, photograph every two weeks, and compare the photos rather than your memory. ## Frequently Asked Questions ### What is the difference between PIH and PIE? PIH (post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation) is brown, tan, or grayish and is caused by excess melanin left behind after inflammation. PIE (post-inflammatory erythema) is pink, red, or purple and is caused by dilated or damaged blood vessels. Press a clear glass against the mark: if the color temporarily blanches and returns, it is PIE; if the color does not change, it is PIH. They need different ingredients, so identifying which you have is the single most useful step you can take. If your marks are red rather than brown, read our guide to [Korean skincare for PIE acne scars and texture](https://www.seoulsister.com/blog/best-korean-skincare-for-pie-acne-scars-and-texture). ### How long does PIH take to fade with Korean skincare? Most people see meaningful improvement between 8 and 16 weeks of consistent use, with the first visible changes around week 4 to 8 on newer marks. Deeper or older pigmentation can take six months to a year, and PIH on deeper skin tones tends to be more persistent. Daily sunscreen is the largest single variable in that timeline, because UV exposure actively re-darkens spots faster than topical actives can fade them. ### Which ingredient is best for PIH: tranexamic acid, niacinamide, arbutin, or vitamin C? They work through different mechanisms, so the best choice depends on your skin. Tranexamic acid interrupts the signal that tells pigment cells to produce melanin and is well tolerated by sensitive skin. Niacinamide blocks pigment being transferred into surface skin cells and also strengthens the barrier. Alpha-arbutin and vitamin C inhibit the melanin-producing enzyme directly, with vitamin C adding daytime antioxidant protection but carrying the highest irritation risk. A practical starting pair is tranexamic acid or niacinamide plus daily sunscreen, adding a third active only once your skin is comfortable. ### Does PIH go away on its own? Often yes, but slowly. Because PIH is a pigment deposit in structurally intact skin rather than a true scar, it typically clears without treatment over several months to a couple of years. Targeted ingredients and consistent sun protection compress that timeline considerably. Sun exposure and picking at spots both extend it, sometimes indefinitely. ### Is PIH more common on deeper skin tones? Yes. More active melanocytes means a stronger pigment response to the same amount of inflammation, so PIH on deeper skin tones is generally darker, more common, and slower to fade. The practical consequences are that early treatment matters more, and that harsh treatments carry real risk, because irritation from aggressive exfoliation or strong peels can trigger additional pigmentation and worsen the problem. Gentle, consistent actives paired with rigorous sun protection are the safer and more effective route. ### Can I treat PIH and active acne at the same time? Yes, but sequence matters. Get the active breakouts under control first, because ongoing inflammation keeps generating new pigment faster than you can fade the old. Once breakouts are calmer, introduce brightening actives gradually. Niacinamide is the most compatible with acne treatment, since it supports the barrier and is unlikely to conflict with the ingredients you are already using. ## The Bottom Line PIH is one of the more solvable skin concerns, because the pigment sits in skin that has already healed. The pattern that works is unglamorous: identify that your marks are genuinely brown rather than red, pick one or two pigment-pathway ingredients rather than five, wear sunscreen every single day without exceptions, and stop picking at spots while they are still active. Then give it three months before judging results. Almost every PIH routine that fails, fails because it was abandoned at week six. If you are unsure whether you are dealing with PIH or PIE, or want help checking whether the actives in your current routine conflict with each other, ask Yuri.
